title: KMS: keys, envelope encryption and customer-managed keys

videos.script: Encrypting data is easy. The hard question is who holds the key, and who may use it. {{who}} In AWS the answer is KMS. A key in KMS never leaves it. Programs ask KMS to use the key, and every request is checked against a policy and recorded. {{kms}} You will make a key of your own, encrypt a short note with it, and see that the ciphertext names its key, and that a context, which is not secret, is still required to decrypt. {{context}} Then envelope encryption, which is how S3 and every database encrypt terabytes with a key that takes four kilobytes: one request to KMS per file, whatever its size. {{envelope}} You will rotate the key, schedule its deletion, and see the one thing moto gets wrong here, which is the reason the waiting period exists. {{delete}} And you will price it: a dollar a key, three cents per ten thousand requests, and the bucket setting that cuts those requests by ninety-nine percent. {{price}}
